To edit a layout from the admin without forking the theme, call core.layout.detach to flip its source to 'custom'. core.layout.reattach reverses that and restores the theme template.

The same pair exists for content blocks: core.block_types.detach / core.block_types.reattach.

docs.title: theme.json Reference
docs.summary: Every field the theme manifest accepts.

fields.body:
Required fields

  • name (string) — display name.
  • version (string) — semver.
  • description (string) — long-form description.
  • author (string).

The slug is implicit — it's the directory name under themes/. core.theme.deploy validates that the package's directory name is a clean slug.

Layouts, partials, blocks, templates

Each is an array of declarations. Each declaration carries a slug, a human name, the relative path under the theme to the source file, and its field schema.

{
  "name":        "Squilla",
  "version":     "0.2.0",
  "description": "The marketing site theme.",
  "author":      "Squilla",

  "styles":      [ { "src": "styles/theme.css" } ],
  "scripts":     [ { "src": "scripts/theme.js" } ],

  "layouts": [
    { "slug": "default", "name": "Default", "file": "layouts/default.html", "is_default": true,
      "field_schema": [] }
  ],
  "partials": [
    { "slug": "site-header", "name": "Site header", "file": "partials/site-header.html",
      "field_schema": [
        { "key": "cta_label", "type": "text", "default": "Get started" }
      ] }
  ],
  "blocks": [
    { "slug": "hero", "name": "Hero", "dir": "blocks/hero" }
  ],
  "templates": [
    { "slug": "homepage", "name": "Marketing homepage", "file": "templates/homepage.json" }
  ],

  "image_sizes":  [ { "slug": "thumb", "width": 320, "height": 240, "crop": "center" } ],
  "assets":       [ { "key": "logo", "src": "assets/logo.svg", "alt": "Squilla logo" } ],

  "settings_pages": [
    { "slug": "brand",  "name": "Brand",  "file": "settings/brand.json"  },
    { "slug": "footer", "name": "Footer", "file": "settings/footer.json" }
  ]
}

Field schema convention

This trips everyone up. Field schema entries on layouts, partials, and blocks use "key":. Field schema entries on node types registered through Tengo (core/nodetypes.register) use "name":. Mixing them produces empty admin inputs even when fields_data is correct, because the form renderer matches values against the wrong key.

fields.label: HEADS UP
fields.body: block.json / theme.json field_schema → "key". Tengo nodetypes.register field_schema → "name". The MCP tool core.guide has this fact in its gotchas table.

Validation

core.theme.checklist walks a theme and flags missing is_default, undeclared assets used in seed data, layouts referenced from templates/*.json that don't exist, and missing test_data on blocks. Run it before shipping.

docs.title: Layouts and Partials
docs.summary: Page chrome, partials, template context, and the helper toolbox.

fields.body:
Layouts

Layouts live in layouts/*.html and are referenced by slug from theme.json. The active node's layout is selected via the cascade described in the overview. A layout must include {{.node.blocks_html}} somewhere — that's the rendered block sequence for the current node. Most layouts also call {{renderLayoutBlock "site-header"}} and {{renderLayoutBlock "site-footer"}} for the chrome partials.

Layout context

Inside a layout you have:

  • .app — site-wide context: HeadStyles, HeadScripts, FootScripts, HeadMeta, Settings, Languages, CurrentLang, BlockStyles, BlockScripts, ThemeURL, Menus.
  • .node — current node: ID, Status, Title, Slug, FullURL, FeaturedImage, Excerpt, Taxonomies, BlocksHTML, Fields, SEO, NodeType, LanguageCode, Translations.
  • .user — viewer info: LoggedIn, ID, Email, Role, FullName.
  • .theme_settings — values for the active theme's settings pages.

Partial context

A partial sees the full layout context plus .partial.* — its own field values resolved per-page from the node's layout_data[partial_slug] with a fallback chain: explicit value → default_from reference → blank. Use partials for chrome that varies subtly per page (e.g. a hero override on the homepage but not on blog posts).

Block view context

Inside a block view.html you see only the block's own field values at root. There is no .app, no .node, no .user. Theme settings are reachable via the themeSetting and themeSettingsPage template helpers, which the renderer injects into the per-block FuncMap. This isolation is intentional: blocks are atomic, cacheable, and have to render correctly in core.render.block previews where no node exists.

fields.label: HEADS UP
fields.body: Need node data inside a block? Lift it through fields_data from the seed or the editor — copy the URL, the title, the image, whatever you need. Or render the block at the layout level via renderLayoutBlock and treat it as a partial.

Settings access

Site settings are stored with dotted keys (e.g. squilla.brand.name). Go templates can't dot-traverse arbitrary keys, so use the setting helper or index:

{{- $s := .app.settings -}}
<title>{{ index $s "squilla.brand.name" }}</title>

{{/* OR the dedicated helper */}}
<meta name="description" content="{{ setting "squilla.brand.tagline" }}">

Template function reference

The renderer registers a FuncMap before parsing every template. The catalogue:

  • setting, mustSetting — read site settings (mustSetting errors if missing).
  • themeSetting, themeSettingsPage — read theme-scoped settings (in block context).
  • renderLayoutBlock — inject a partial. Recursion-bounded at depth 5.
  • filter — apply a Tengo filter chain: {{ filter "node.title" .node.Title }}.
  • event — fire an event-with-result and inline the returned HTML. Used for forms: {{ event "forms:render" (dict "form_id" "contact") }}.
  • image_url, image_srcset — resolve a media object to an URL or a responsive srcset.
  • safeHTML, raw, safeURL — bypass auto-escaping (sanitiser still runs upstream for richtext fields).
  • json, dict, list, seq — small data utilities.
  • split, lastWord, beforeLastWord — string helpers used by typography flourishes.
  • add, sub, mod — arithmetic.
  • deref — dereference a pointer to its underlying value (rare; mostly for FeaturedImage).

Menus inside templates

Menus are exposed as .app.menus["slug"] with an items array. Each item carries title, url, target, and optional children.

{{- $nav := index .app.menus "main-nav" -}}
<nav>
{{- range $nav.items -}}
  <a href="{{ .url }}" {{ if .target }}target="{{ .target }}"{{ end }}>{{ .title }}</a>
{{- end -}}
</nav>

fields.label: HEADS UP
fields.body: Menu items render via .title, NOT .label. The Tengo input to menus.upsert uses label:, but the rendered shape uses title. Templates that read {{.label}} will silently render an empty string.

Layout <head> checklist

Every layout's <head> should include the four kernel-managed fragments so SEO, fonts, and block-scoped CSS land correctly:

<head>
  {{ safeHTML .app.head_meta }}    {{/* meta + canonical + og + twitter */}}
  {{ safeHTML .app.head_styles }}  {{/* theme CSS bundles */}}
  {{ safeHTML .app.block_styles }} {{/* per-block scoped CSS */}}
  {{ safeHTML .app.head_scripts }} {{/* head-injected JS, e.g. analytics */}}
</head>

404

If your theme ships a layouts/404.html, the kernel uses it for unmatched routes. It receives the layout context with .node set to a synthetic 404 node. Without one, the kernel renders a built-in fallback.

docs.title: Authoring Blocks
docs.summary: block.json, view.html, scoped CSS/JS, and the test_data invariant.

fields.body:
Anatomy of a block

A block lives under themes/<t>/blocks/<slug>/ and consists of two required files plus two optional ones.

  • block.json — slug, label, icon, field_schema, test_data, optional cache_output.
  • view.html — Go template that consumes the field values at root.
  • style.css — block-scoped CSS, injected via .app.block_styles (optional).
  • script.js — block-scoped JS, injected via .app.block_scripts (optional).

The field schema

Every field has a type, a key, and per-type configuration. Common shapes:

{
  "slug": "hero",
  "label": "Hero",
  "icon": "Stars",
  "field_schema": [
    { "key": "heading",   "type": "text",     "required": true, "width": "full" },
    { "key": "subhead",   "type": "textarea", "width": "full" },
    { "key": "image",     "type": "image",    "width": "half"  },
    { "key": "cta",       "type": "link",     "width": "half"  },
    { "key": "items",     "type": "repeater",
      "sub_fields": [
        { "key": "label",  "type": "text" },
        { "key": "icon",   "type": "text" }
      ]
    }
  ],
  "test_data": {
    "heading": "The CMS where AI does the work",
    "subhead": "Activate a theme. The CMS reorganises itself around it.",
    "image":   { "src": "theme-asset:hero", "alt": "Squilla" },
    "cta":     { "label": "Get started", "url": "/docs", "target": "_self" },
    "items":   [
      { "label": "50ms TTFB", "icon": "Zap" },
      { "label": "AI-native", "icon": "Sparkles" }
    ]
  }
}

fields.label: HEADS UP
fields.body: block.json field_schema entries use "key":. The same fields registered via Tengo core/nodetypes.register use "name":. Mismatching the two produces empty admin inputs.

The test_data invariant

Every key in field_schema must have a corresponding entry in test_data. The admin renders test_data as the live preview when an editor opens a block they haven't touched yet, and core.render.block uses it as the default when no fields are passed. A missing entry shows as a broken empty area; core.theme.checklist flags this.

No fallback values

If you write {{ or .heading "default" }}, you're hiding a data bug.

Fallback values mask the case where seed data was supposed to populate the field but didn't. Pass real defaults via fields_data in the seed and let templates fail visibly when something is wrong. The block renderer catches per-block errors and renders a red badge in place of the failed block — your page still loads, the bug is obvious.

Field types

The admin understands these field types out of the box: text, textarea, richtext, number, email, url, color, range, date, select, radio, checkbox, toggle, link, group, repeater, term, node, node_type_select. Extensions can register additional types via the manifest's admin_ui.field_types[] — image, media, file, gallery all come from media-manager; vibe-form comes from forms. Get the canonical list with core.field_types.list.

Per-field configuration

Every field accepts: required, default, placeholder, help, and width (full | half | third). The help string is surfaced through MCP so an AI agent understands what the field is for — write helpful copy.

Caching

Set "cache_output": true on a block to opt into render-result caching. The kernel keys the cache by block type slug + a hash of the field values. Use this for blocks whose output is pure-functional in their fields (e.g. a marketing card with no node-derived data).

view.html

Block templates are Go templates with the per-block FuncMap. Field values are at the root.

<section class="hero">
  <h1>{{ .heading }}</h1>
  {{ if .subhead }}<p>{{ .subhead }}</p>{{ end }}
  {{ if .image }}
    <img src="{{ image_url .image "hero" }}" alt="{{ .image.alt }}">
  {{ end }}
  {{ if .cta }}
    <a href="{{ .cta.url }}" target="{{ .cta.target }}">{{ .cta.label }}</a>
  {{ end }}
  <ul>
  {{ range .items }}
    <li data-icon="{{ .icon }}">{{ .label }}</li>
  {{ end }}
  </ul>
</section>

Scoped CSS/JS

style.css and script.js next to view.html are auto-injected when the block is used on a page. The kernel deduplicates: a block used five times on a page injects its CSS once. Do not write global selectors — scope to the block's root element. The doc-codeblock block's style.css is a good reference.

docs.title: Theme Settings
docs.summary: Editor-driven, per-page theme configuration with full custom-field support.

fields.body:
What this is

Theme settings are an editor-friendly way to expose theme configuration without inventing site settings keys. You declare settings pages in theme.json; each page gets a JSON schema file describing its fields; the admin renders one editor screen per page under /admin/theme-settings/<page>; templates and Tengo read values at runtime.

Use site settings (core.settings.set) for cross-cutting config (brand name, default language). Use theme settings for theme-shaped UI knobs (header style, footer columns, hero variant).

Declaring pages

"settings_pages": [
  { "slug": "brand",  "name": "Brand",  "file": "settings/brand.json",  "icon": "Sparkles" },
  { "slug": "footer", "name": "Footer", "file": "settings/footer.json", "icon": "AlignBottom" }
]

Per-page schema

Each page schema is an object with fields: an array of field definitions using the same field-type vocabulary as blocks (key, type, label, required, default, help, width).

{
  "fields": [
    { "key": "primary_color", "type": "color",  "label": "Primary",   "default": "#1d4ed8" },
    { "key": "logo",          "type": "image",  "label": "Logo"       },
    { "key": "tagline",       "type": "text",   "label": "Tagline"    }
  ]
}

Reading from layouts and partials

The render context exposes .theme_settings.<page>.<key>:

{{- $brand := .theme_settings.brand -}}
<img src="{{ image_url $brand.logo "thumb" }}" alt="">
<p>{{ $brand.tagline }}</p>

Reading from blocks

Block view context excludes .theme_settings. Use the themeSetting helper instead:

<section style="--brand: {{ themeSetting "brand" "primary_color" }}">
  <a href="{{ .cta.url }}">{{ .cta.label }}</a>
</section>

Reading from Tengo

The core/theme_settings module exposes active_theme(), pages(), get(page, key), and all(page). Reads require the theme_settings:read capability — which the default theme capability set already includes.

ts := import("core/theme_settings")
logo := ts.get("brand", "logo")
// logo is the same media-object shape used elsewhere

Storage and lifecycle

Theme settings are stored in site_settings with keys of the form theme:<slug>:<page>:<field_key>. Activation snapshots the schema in-memory; updating theme.json requires a re-activation (or core.theme.rescan) to pick up new fields. Field-type changes do not migrate values — if you change a field from text to select, old text values stay in the database and the admin renders an empty select. Plan field changes carefully.

Image fields

Image fields store the same media-object shape as blocks ({src, alt, width, height, ...}). Use image_url in templates to derive size-specific URLs.

docs.title: Scripting with Tengo
docs.summary: The embedded Tengo scripting engine — when, why, and how.

fields.body:
Why Tengo

Tengo is a small, sandboxed scripting language. Squilla embeds a Tengo VM so themes and Tengo-only extensions can run logic without a Go compile step. Memory and execution time are bounded; the sandbox blocks filesystem and network access except through whitelisted modules. Per-invocation limits: 50,000 allocations, 10 seconds wall-clock.

Where Tengo runs

  • Theme entry script — scripts/theme.tengo, executed once on theme activation. Top-level statements run; there is no exported main. Used for seeding nodes, registering node types, taxonomies, settings, menus, and wiring filters.
  • Extension entry script — scripts/extension.tengo, executed once on extension activation. Same pattern as the theme entry script. Used for subscribing to events, registering filters and routes.
  • Handler scripts — referenced by event/filter/route registrations, executed on every dispatch. Receive the input via implicit globals (event, value, request), set response to return a value.

Imports

Tengo supports two import styles. core/* imports load built-in modules. Relative imports (./setup/nodetypes) load source modules from the theme's or extension's scripts/ directory.

// Built-in modules (always available)
log      := import("core/log")
nodes    := import("core/nodes")
events   := import("core/events")

// Local modules (relative to scripts/)
setup_nt := import("./setup/nodetypes")
seeds    := import("./seeds/pages")

log.info("squilla theme starting")
setup_nt.run()
seeds.run()

Idempotency

The theme entry script runs on every activation, including after a server restart. Seeds must be idempotent — query by slug before creating, no duplicate inserts. The pattern across the in-tree themes is a seeds/*.tengo file with helper functions that check existence first.

nodes := import("core/nodes")

ensure_page := func(slug, title, layout, blocks) {
    res := nodes.query({ node_type: "page", slug: slug, limit: 1 })
    if !is_error(res) && res.total > 0 { return }
    nodes.create({
        title:       title,
        slug:        slug,
        node_type:   "page",
        status:      "published",
        layout:      layout,
        blocks_data: blocks
    })
}

fields.label: HEADS UP
fields.body: Don't try log.error — error is reserved in Tengo. Use log.err instead. The other levels (info, warn, debug) work as expected.

Capabilities

Theme scripts run with a default capability set that covers reads and writes for nodes, node types, taxonomies, terms, settings, menus, filters, routes, log, http, files, and theme settings — but not raw data store, media, or email. Extension scripts inherit whatever the manifest's capabilities array declares.

Capability checks happen at the CoreAPI boundary. A Tengo call to core/data.exec from a theme script returns an error rather than executing the SQL.

What you can't do

  • Open arbitrary network connections — use core/http.
  • Read arbitrary files — use core/assets, scoped to the theme/extension root.
  • Spawn subprocesses or shell out.
  • Write files outside the storage path conventions of core/files.

docs.title: core/* Module Reference
docs.summary: Every Tengo module the engine exposes, with signatures and gotchas.

fields.body:
Loading order

The Tengo adapter registers built-in modules at engine boot. They are always available with import("core/<name>"); capability checks fire at call time, not import time, so importing a module you don't have permissions for is harmless.

core/log

Structured leveled logging. Caller info (theme/extension slug) is auto-prefixed.

  • log.info(message, fields?)
  • log.warn(message, fields?)
  • log.debug(message, fields?)
  • log.err(message, fields?) — alias because error is reserved.

core/nodes

  • nodes.get(id) → Node object, or error.
  • nodes.query({node_type?, status?, language_code?, slug?, search?, limit?, offset?, order_by?, parent_id?}) → {nodes: [...], total: N}.
  • nodes.create({title, node_type, status, slug?, layout?, language_code?, fields_data?, blocks_data?, seo_settings?, featured_image?, taxonomies?, excerpt?}) → Node.
  • nodes.update(id, partial_input) → Node.
  • nodes.delete(id) → undefined.

core/nodetypes

  • nodetypes.register({slug, label, label_plural, icon?, description?, taxonomies?, field_schema?, url_prefixes?}) → NodeType.
  • nodetypes.get(slug) → NodeType.
  • nodetypes.list() → [NodeType].

fields.label: HEADS UP
fields.body: nodetypes.register field_schema entries use "name":. block.json field_schema entries use "key":. Mixing them produces empty admin inputs.

core/taxonomies

  • taxonomies.register({slug, label, label_plural, hierarchical?, show_ui?, node_types?, field_schema?})
  • taxonomies.get(slug) / taxonomies.list()
  • taxonomies.update(slug, partial) / taxonomies.delete(slug)

core/terms

  • terms.list(node_type, taxonomy) → [Term].
  • terms.get(id) → Term.
  • terms.create({node_type, taxonomy, slug, name, description?, parent_id?}) → Term.
  • terms.update(id, updates_map) → Term.
  • terms.delete(id) → undefined.

core/menus

  • menus.upsert({slug, name, items: [{label, url|page, target?, children?}]}) → Menu. Idempotent on slug. page: "<node-slug>" resolves to the node's id at upsert time, so renaming the page later doesn't break the menu.
  • menus.get(slug) / menus.list() / menus.delete(slug)

core/settings

  • settings.get(key) → string.
  • settings.set(key, value) — emits setting.updated event with {key, language_code}.
  • settings.all(prefix?) → {key: value, ...}.

core/theme_settings

  • theme_settings.active_theme() → slug.
  • theme_settings.pages() → [{slug, name, icon}].
  • theme_settings.get(page_slug, field_key) — requires theme_settings:read.
  • theme_settings.all(page_slug) → field map.

core/events

  • events.emit(action, payload?) — fire-and-forget, non-blocking.
  • events.on(action, script_path, priority=50) — subscribe.
  • events.subscribe(action, script_path, priority=10) — same as on, just a lower default priority.

core/filters

  • filters.add(name, script_path, priority=10) — register a filter handler. Lower priorities run first.

core/routes

  • routes.register(method, path, script_path) — mount an HTTP handler. Paths containing a dot mount at the top level (e.g. /sitemap.xml); other paths mount under /api/theme/.

core/wellknown

  • wellknown.register(path, script_path) — handler under /.well-known/<path>. Trailing * is a prefix wildcard.

core/http

  • http.get(url, options?) / http.post(...) / http.put(...) / http.delete(...)
  • http.fetch(method, url, options?) — generic.

Options: {headers: {...}, body: "...", timeout: 30} (timeout in seconds, capped by the 10-second script timeout).

Returns {status_code, body, headers, error?}.

core/assets

  • assets.read(rel_path) → string. Path is resolved against the theme/extension root; absolute paths and traversal escapes are rejected.
  • assets.exists(rel_path) → bool.

core/helpers

  • helpers.json_encode(value) → string (returns "null" on error).
  • helpers.json_decode(string) → any (returns undefined on parse failure).

core/routing

Available only inside render-scope scripts (filter/event handlers running during a render).

  • routing.is_404() → bool.
  • routing.is_homepage() → bool.
  • routing.site_setting(key) → string.

Standard library

The Tengo stdlib is enabled: fmt, json, math, times, rand, enum, text, os (limited subset). See the upstream Tengo docs for signatures.

docs.title: Events and Filters
docs.summary: Hook into the event bus, transform values via the filter chain, mount HTTP routes.

fields.body:
Events vs filters: pick the right tool

  • Events are fire-and-forget. Use them for cache invalidation, analytics, sending email, recomputing derived state. Subscribers run after the originating call returns; the caller never sees the result.
  • Filters are synchronous and ordered. Each handler receives a value, returns a value, and the next handler in the chain receives the previous handler's output. Use them for transforming HTML, post-processing search results, mutating settings before they're written.

Subscribing to events

events := import("core/events")

// Default priority 50; lower runs first.
events.on("node.created",       "./handlers/on_node_created")
events.on("page.served",        "./handlers/on_page_served", 90)
events.subscribe("setting.updated", "./handlers/on_setting")

Inside the handler

The handler script receives a global event object with action and payload fields. Set response to return a value (used by event-with-result patterns like forms:render); for fire-and-forget events the response is ignored.

log := import("core/log")
log.info("node.created", { id: event.payload.id, type: event.payload.node_type })
response = { ok: true }

Standard kernel events

  • node.created / node.updated / node.deleted — fired after writes. Payload contains the node's id, slug, node_type, language_code.
  • setting.updated — payload {key, language_code}. Fired after core/settings.set.
  • theme.activated / theme.deactivated — payload includes {name, path, version, assets, image_sizes}.
  • extension.activated / extension.deactivated — payload contains the manifest.
  • email.send — synchronous (uses PublishSync). Provider extensions (smtp-provider, resend-provider) subscribe to deliver the email.
  • media.uploaded — fired when a new media file is registered.
  • page.served — fired after every public page render.

Extensions emit additional events. Inspect extensions/forms, extensions/media-manager to see custom events in use.

Filter chain

Filters are registered with filters.add(name, script_path, priority=10). Lower priorities run first. Each handler reads value and sets response; response becomes value for the next handler. The kernel does not ship any built-in filters — every filter is theme- or extension-defined.

filters := import("core/filters")
filters.add("list_posts",       "./filters/list_posts")
filters.add("node.title",       "./filters/site_title_suffix", 90)

// value is whatever the caller passed.
response = string(value) + " — Squilla"

Applying filters from templates

The filter template helper invokes a filter chain by name:
<title>{{ filter "node.title" .node.Title }}</title>

HTTP routes

routes.register(method, path, script_path) mounts a handler. Paths containing a dot (/sitemap.xml) mount at the top level; other paths mount under /api/theme/ for theme scripts. Extension scripts share the same rule but should prefer declared public_routes in the manifest.

Inside a route handler, request is the input ({method, path, query, params, headers, body, ip}) and response is the output ({status?, headers?, body?, html?, text?, content_type?}).
response = { status: 200, body: "ok", content_type: "text/plain" }

fields.label: NOTE
fields.body: Filter handlers and event handlers are loaded once when the entry script registers them; the script body runs on every dispatch. Don't put expensive setup in handler bodies — keep them small.

Lifetime & ownership

Handlers registered by an entry script are tagged with that script's owner (theme slug or extension slug). Re-activating an extension unloads its handlers and re-registers them. Two extensions can subscribe to the same event with no conflict; the priority decides ordering.

docs.title: CoreAPI Reference
docs.summary: The 46 methods on the Go CoreAPI surface, grouped by domain.

fields.body:
The CoreAPI surface

The CoreAPI is the single Go interface that exposes all kernel capabilities to plugins, scripts, and the MCP server. 46 methods across 14 domains. Three adapters wrap it: Tengo modules, the gRPC SquillaHost service, and the internal Go interface used by core handlers.

Capability guard

Every method is wrapped by NewCapabilityGuard. Calls from extensions or scripts are checked against the manifest's declared capabilities. Internal kernel callers (and the MCP dispatcher, which uses an internal-typed caller) bypass the guard. There is no override.

fields.label: HEADS UP
fields.body: MCP runs every tool invocation as an internal caller, so the CoreAPI guard does not enforce token-level permissions for MCP. Token-level enforcement happens via the scope gate in MCP dispatch (read | content | full).

Domains and methods

Nodes (5)

  • GetNode(ctx, id) → Node — nodes:read
  • QueryNodes(ctx, query) → NodeList — nodes:read
  • CreateNode(ctx, input) → Node — nodes:write
  • UpdateNode(ctx, id, input) → Node — nodes:write
  • DeleteNode(ctx, id) → error — nodes:delete

Node Types (5)

  • RegisterNodeType, UpdateNodeType, DeleteNodeType — nodetypes:write
  • GetNodeType, ListNodeTypes — nodetypes:read

Taxonomies (5) + Terms (5)

  • Taxonomies — RegisterTaxonomy, UpdateTaxonomy, DeleteTaxonomy (write); GetTaxonomy, ListTaxonomies (read).
  • Terms — ListTerms, GetTerm (read); CreateTerm, UpdateTerm (nodes:write); DeleteTerm (nodes:delete).
  • ListTaxonomyTerms(ctx, nodeType, taxonomy) → []string — convenience read.

Settings (6)

  • GetSetting, GetSettings(prefix), GetSettingLoc, GetSettingsLoc — settings:read
  • SetSetting, SetSettingLoc — settings:write (emits setting.updated)

Events (2)

  • Emit(ctx, action, payload) → error — events:emit
  • Subscribe(ctx, action, handler) → UnsubscribeFunc — events:subscribe

Email (1)

  • SendEmail(ctx, req) → error — email:send. Internally fans out via email.send sync event; provider extensions subscribe.

Menus (6)

  • GetMenu, GetMenus — menus:read
  • CreateMenu, UpdateMenu, UpsertMenu — menus:write
  • DeleteMenu — menus:delete

Routes (2)

  • RegisterRoute(ctx, method, path, meta), RemoveRoute — routes:register

Filters (2)

  • RegisterFilter(ctx, name, priority, handler) — filters:register
  • ApplyFilters(ctx, name, value) → any — filters:apply

Media (4)

  • UploadMedia — media:write
  • GetMedia, QueryMedia — media:read
  • DeleteMedia — media:delete

Users (2, read-only)

  • GetUser, QueryUsers — users:read

HTTP (1)

  • Fetch(ctx, req) → FetchResponse — http:fetch. Outbound HTTP from extensions; default 30-second timeout.

Log (1)

  • Log(ctx, level, message, fields) → error — log:write. Levels: info, warn, debug, err.

Data Store (6)

  • DataGet, DataQuery — data:read
  • DataCreate, DataUpdate, DataExec — data:write
  • DataDelete — data:delete (falls back to data:write)

File Storage (2)

  • StoreFile — files:write
  • DeleteFile — files:delete

Capability matrix

The 28 distinct capability strings span 13 domains. Internal callers bypass the guard; everyone else must declare what they intend to use. The full matrix:

  • nodes — read, write, delete
  • nodetypes — read, write
  • settings — read, write
  • events — emit, subscribe
  • email — send
  • menus — read, write, delete
  • routes — register
  • filters — register, apply
  • media — read, write, delete
  • users — read
  • http — fetch
  • log — write
  • data — read, write, delete
  • files — write, delete
  • admin_access — gates the admin proxy route (extension-level).

Data store table scoping

Two layers of access control on the data store CoreAPI:

  1. Hard-coded kernel-private deny list — users, sessions, password_reset_tokens, roles, role_capabilities, audit_log, schema_migrations, site_settings, mcp_tokens, mcp_audit_log, mcp_token_audit, languages. Denied unconditionally for non-internal callers.
  2. Per-extension allowlist — the manifest's data_owned_tables array. Calls outside both lists are denied.

MCP runs as internal, so MCP tools see all tables. Direct extension calls are gated.

Raw SQL

DataExec(ctx, sql, args...) runs arbitrary SQL. It's protected by both the capability guard and a kernel env flag — set SQUILLA_MCP_ALLOW_RAW_SQL=1 to make core.data.exec visible from MCP. The CoreAPI method itself remains callable from internal callers without the env flag.

docs.title: MCP Server
docs.summary: AI-native control plane: transports, auth, scoping, audit log.

fields.body:
What MCP gives you

The Model Context Protocol server exposes the CoreAPI as a structured tool surface. An AI agent can drive the entire CMS through ~86 typed tools across 18 domains — without filesystem or shell access. Every operation is a typed call with a typed response.

Activate a theme. The CMS reorganises itself around it. No restart.— core.theme.activate

Transports

Two transports are supported: stdio for local agents (Claude Desktop, Cursor, the Anthropic mcp CLI) and HTTP for remote agents. Configure under mcp.transport in config.yaml.

Authentication

Bearer tokens issued at /admin/settings/tokens. Tokens carry one of three scopes:

  • read — read-only tools (e.g. core.node.query, core.theme.list, core.render.*).
  • content — read tools plus content writes (nodes, terms, menus, media uploads).
  • full — everything, including theme/extension activation, data store writes, raw SQL (when enabled).

fields.label: HEADS UP
fields.body: Scope gates are enforced in MCP dispatch, NOT against the per-method capability guard. CoreAPI capability strings are an architectural feature — for MCP, the scope decides everything. Pick scopes carefully when issuing tokens.

The core.guide meta-tool

Always start with core.guide. It returns a goal→tool decision tree, the canonical data shapes, naming conventions, common gotchas, an editing playbook, and a snapshot of current CMS state (active theme, node types, recent nodes, sections per node type) — plus a tool index of all 86 tools with class and short description. One call replaces ~10 discovery calls.

Pass a topic to narrow the recipe section: pages, editing, blocks, themes, taxonomies, media, extensions.

Resource URIs

The MCP server exposes structured resource URIs alongside tools. Useful for fetching context that would be awkward to express as a tool call.

  • squilla://nodes/<id> — full node JSON.
  • squilla://themes/<slug> — theme manifest + DB row.
  • squilla://extensions/<slug> — extension manifest + DB row.
  • squilla://guidelines/themes — onboarding guidelines for theme authors (machine-readable JSON + Markdown).
  • squilla://guidelines/extensions — same shape for extension authors.
  • squilla://guidelines/onboarding — generic onboarding markdown.

Audit log

Every MCP call is recorded in mcp_audit_log with token id, tool name, args hash (SHA-256), status (ok | error | denied), error code, and duration. Writes are buffered (channel size 256) and flushed asynchronously; overflow drops with a warning. Retention is configurable via the mcp_audit_retention_days setting (default 90).

There is no admin UI for browsing the audit log — query mcp_audit_log directly via the data store tools or psql.

Hot-deploy tools

core.theme.deploy and core.extension.deploy accept a base64-encoded zip and unpack it into themes/ / extensions/ via an atomic directory swap. 50 MB cap per call. With activate=true the new package is registered AND activated in the same call — no server restart, no human in the loop.

core.theme.deploy({
  body_base64: "...<base64 zip>...",
  activate:    true
})

fields.label: NOTE
fields.body: Plugin binaries inside an extension zip must already be compiled for the host's OS/arch. The deploy step does not cross-compile. Build on the same platform as your kernel runtime, or use Docker buildx.

docs.title: MCP Tool Catalog
docs.summary: Every MCP tool, grouped by domain, with parameters and class.

fields.body:
How tools are classified

Each MCP tool is assigned a class — read, content, or full — that the dispatch layer uses to gate by token scope. Read-only tools surface to all tokens; content tools require content or full; full-class tools require full (theme/extension activation, data store writes, raw SQL).

Nodes — 8 tools

  • core.node.get (read) — {id}
  • core.node.query (read) — {node_type, status, language_code, slug, search, limit, offset, order_by, parent_id, tax_query}
  • core.node.create (content) — full input shape with blocks_data, fields_data, seo_settings, taxonomies, featured_image
  • core.node.update (content) — partial input by id
  • core.node.delete (content)
  • core.node.revisions (read) — list snapshots
  • core.node.revision_restore (content)
  • core.node.update_many (content) — bulk update with filters; supports only_when_null_layout_slug for migrations.

Node types — 5 tools

  • core.nodetype.list, core.nodetype.get (read)
  • core.nodetype.create, core.nodetype.update, core.nodetype.delete (full)

Taxonomies — 5 tools, Terms — 5 tools

  • Taxonomies: list, get (read); create, update, delete (full).
  • Terms: list, get (read); create, update, delete (content).

Menus — 6 tools

  • core.menu.get, core.menu.list (read)
  • core.menu.create, core.menu.update, core.menu.upsert, core.menu.delete (content)

Settings — 3 tools

  • core.settings.get, core.settings.list (read)
  • core.settings.set (full)

Media — 5 tools

  • core.media.upload (content) — {filename, mime_type, body_base64}
  • core.media.import_url (content) — fetches a remote URL into the library
  • core.media.get, core.media.query (read)
  • core.media.delete (content)

Files — 2 tools

  • core.files.store (content) — {path, body_base64}; storage relative to storage/
  • core.files.delete (content)

Data — 6 tools

  • core.data.get, core.data.query (read)
  • core.data.create, core.data.update, core.data.delete (content)
  • core.data.exec (full, env-gated by SQUILLA_MCP_ALLOW_RAW_SQL=1) — raw SQL with parameters

fields.label: HEADS UP
fields.body: core.data.query supports where, search, order_by, limit, offset, raw, args. Kernel-private tables (users, sessions, etc.) are unconditionally denied unless scope=full.

Themes — 9 tools

  • core.theme.list, core.theme.get, core.theme.active, core.theme.standards, core.theme.checklist (read)
  • core.theme.activate, core.theme.deactivate, core.theme.deploy, core.theme.rescan (full)

Block types — 7 tools

  • core.block_types.list, core.block_types.get (read)
  • core.block_types.create, core.block_types.update, core.block_types.delete, core.block_types.detach, core.block_types.reattach (full)

Layouts — 7 tools

  • core.layout.list, core.layout.get (read)
  • core.layout.create, core.layout.update, core.layout.delete, core.layout.detach, core.layout.reattach (full)

Extensions — 7 tools

  • core.extension.list, core.extension.get, core.extension.standards (read)
